name: Nettle root

card.summary: Stinging nettle root extract, studied for prostate symptoms and promoted as an SHBG binder; the testosterone claim rests on lab work.
card.aka: Urtica dioica root, stinging nettle root extract
card.note: Human trials are in benign prostatic hyperplasia, not free-testosterone or appearance outcomes.

quick.overview:
Nettle root is the root of the stinging nettle (Urtica dioica). Extracts are used in European herbal products for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), and in supplement circles it is promoted as a way to bind sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and so leave more testosterone free.

A randomised trial of one root extract in BPH patients reported symptom improvement over placebo. No human trial was found that tests nettle root for testosterone or appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Laboratory studies have reported that components of nettle root bind SHBG and inhibit its interaction with prostate cell membranes; Grokipedia says that the clinical significance is unclear and unsupported by robust clinical evidence [1]. Lab studies of root extracts also report effects on prostate cell growth and on enzyme activity in prostate tissue [2][3][4].
quick.risks: Grokipedia reports rare mild digestive upset and advises against oral use in pregnancy, and lists possible interactions with diuretics, blood-pressure and diabetes drugs, lithium and warfarin [1]. As an AI-generated source it is unverified.

lead: Nettle root refers to extracts of the roots of Urtica dioica, the common stinging nettle. In bodybuilding and testosterone-optimisation circles it is taken as an 'SHBG binder': proponents say that it reduces the amount of testosterone held by sex hormone-binding globulin, leaving more free hormone to support muscle, recovery, skin and the masculine features users are chasing.[1][6][12]

Root extracts also have a long tradition in German phytotherapy for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) [5]. The laboratory basis for the SHBG idea is that a nettle root lignan, (-)3,4-divanillyltetrahydrofuran, binds human SHBG in crystallographic and binding assays [6]. Grokipedia states that the clinical significance of this for testosterone is unclear and unsupported by robust clinical evidence [1].

The human evidence that exists concerns urinary symptoms of BPH, including a 12-month randomised placebo-controlled trial of a root extract in 246 patients [5]. Forum users, mainly on T Nation, discuss nettle root alongside boron and DIM in threads about high SHBG and low free testosterone [12][13].
infobox: Sold as a herbal / dietary supplement

paras: SHBG is a blood protein that binds sex hormones. Proponents say that a nettle root compound occupying SHBG leaves more testosterone unbound. Laboratory studies reported that lignans from the root, including one with high affinity, bind human SHBG, and that aqueous root extracts inhibit SHBG binding to prostate membranes [1]. A 2020 biochemical study examined interactions between SHBG and nonsteroidal ligands that enhance androgen activity [6].

Other laboratory studies examined root extracts on prostate cell lines, reporting an antiproliferative effect on LNCaP cancer cells [2], inhibition of enzyme activity in BPH tissue [3] and inhibition of induced prostate growth in mice [4]. A 2024 study tested a combined saw palmetto and nettle root extract on prostate hyperplasia and inflammation in rats and human cells [7].
No studies found that test nettle root for testosterone, free testosterone or appearance outcomes.

For BPH, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial of 459 mg of dry nettle root extract (Bazoton-uno) enrolled 246 patients for one year; the International Prostate Symptom Score fell from 18.7 to 13.0 on the extract versus 18.5 to 13.8 on placebo (p=0.0233) [5]. Grokipedia also cites a systematic review of randomised trials reporting improved symptom scores with Urtica extracts and no significant adverse effects versus controls, without giving its year [1].

A randomised controlled trial in Pakistan enrolled 60 men with BPH and assessed clinical and biochemical parameters with a nettle root extract [8]. An earlier double-blind multicentre trial in Warsaw compared two doses of a combined nettle root and Pygeum africanum extract in 134 men aged 53 to 84 with BPH symptoms over 8 weeks, reporting significant improvement in urine flow, residual urine and nocturia after 28 days [9]. A comparison of a combined sabal and urtica extract with finasteride in men with BPH analysed prostate volume and outcomes [10]. A 2025 review of nettle roots summarises their constituents and pharmacology [3].

Grokipedia reports that oral use is generally considered safe up to a year at recommended doses with rare mild gastrointestinal effects, that oral preparations are contraindicated in pregnancy, and that possible interactions include diuretics, antidiabetic and blood-pressure drugs, lithium and warfarin [1]. These statements are from an AI-generated source and are not independently verified here.

Stinging nettle has a long record as a food, fibre and folk-medicine plant. Wikipedia notes its appearance in the 10th-century Nine Herbs Charm, Bronze Age nettle textiles found in Denmark, and use of the roots as a yellow dye.[14] Nettle root extracts developed their medical profile in European herbal medicine for prostate complaints, and a 1996 German review listed Urtica dioica root among phytopharmaceuticals used for BPH.[11] Its adoption by strength-sport and men's-health communities as an SHBG-lowering supplement appears in T Nation threads from 2014 onward.[12][13][15]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and physique communities
paras: T Nation posters describe nettle root, boron, magnesium, vitamin D and DIM as options for people whose lab results show high SHBG and low free testosterone.[12][13][16] One user posted a protocol note listing nettle root and boron for high SHBG; another said that boron and nettle root supplements preceded a decline in their SHBG.[17][18] Contributors also note the root and leaf differ, as a reply thread asked whether a store carries root or leaf extract.[19]

lore.intro: Nettle root is discussed in T Nation threads on SHBG and free testosterone, usually as one of several supplements to try, with some users reporting changes in lab values and others cautioning about its effect on DHT.[12][13][17]

claims.claim: Nettle root binds SHBG and raises free testosterone.
claims.believers: A poster says nettle root and DIM 'decrease bound testosterone, therefore leaving more as free'.[16] Others list nettle root among things that lower SHBG.[12]
claims.experts: Biochemical work shows a nettle root lignan binds human SHBG in vitro, but Grokipedia states that clinical significance is unclear and unsupported by robust clinical evidence; no trial of free testosterone was found.[6][1]

claims.claim: Nettle root lowers measured SHBG in people with high levels.
claims.believers: A user with high SHBG reported that SHBG declined after trying boron and nettle root together.[18]
claims.experts: The anecdote combines two supplements with other changes; no controlled trial in men with high SHBG has been published.[1]

claims.claim: Nettle root inhibits the conversion of testosterone to DHT, which could cause problems for some users.
claims.believers: One T Nation reply advised a man with low testosterone to avoid nettle root because it inhibits T-to-DHT conversion.[20]
claims.experts: Laboratory studies report nettle root extracts affecting prostate cells and enzymes and inhibiting induced prostate growth in mice, and trials in BPH report symptom improvement.[2][3][4][5]

claims.claim: Nettle root shrinks or protects the prostate while on testosterone therapy.
claims.believers: A poster said that nettle root helped prostate comfort when diet and sleep were right.[16]
claims.experts: BPH trials of root extracts, some of them in combination products, report improvement in urinary symptom scores; Grokipedia refers to a systematic review of such trials.[5][9][1]

chain: Root lignans bind SHBG in lab assays
Proponents say more testosterone stays unbound
Support for muscle, recovery and androgen-dependent looks (claimed)
angle.text: Users take nettle root hoping to lower SHBG so that a larger share of their testosterone is free, which they associate with leaner, more muscular and more androgenic looks. The mechanism has laboratory support for SHBG binding; trials in humans have measured prostate symptoms.
